titre: Point Nemo, the Place Farthest From Any Land, and the Satellite Graveyard
accroche: The point in the ocean farthest from any coast is so remote that the ISS sometimes passes closer to it than any shore does.
contenu_vulgarise:
At 48°52.6′ south latitude and 123°23.6′ west longitude, in the middle of the South Pacific, a boat trying to reach the nearest land might almost as well aim for the International Space Station: at some 400 km of altitude, it sometimes passes closer to this point than any shore does. The place has a name, Point Nemo, and an unexpected use: it is where space agencies send their end-of-life satellites and stations to die.

## The Mechanism

The point has nothing remarkable in itself, no undersea relief, no particular current. It is a purely geometric construction: the oceanic pole of inaccessibility, calculated in 1992 by the Croatian-Canadian surveying engineer Hrvoje Lukatela using spatial geometry software, to demonstrate its capabilities on what he called the “longest swim problem.” The calculation looks, among all the points of the world ocean, for the one that maximizes the distance to the nearest emerged lands. The result picks out three shores at almost equal distance: Ducie, in the Pitcairn archipelago, to the north; Motu Nui, an islet off Easter Island, to the northeast; and Maher Island, off Antarctica, to the south. Each lies about 2,688 kilometers from Point Nemo: more than the distance from Paris to Moscow.

This distance matters to another category of travelers: space agencies. A deorbited craft (station, end-of-service satellite, resupply freighter) never burns up entirely in the atmosphere; fragments often survive reentry and fall somewhere. Aiming for Point Nemo, which NASA designates the “South Pacific Oceanic Uninhabited Area” in its transition report on the future of the International Space Station (January 2022), amounts to choosing the place on the globe where this debris is least likely to land on anyone. The Russian station Mir ended there on March 23, 2001, its 130 tons largely disintegrating, the rest plunging into the South Pacific, visible from Fiji; the ISS itself is due to follow the same path by the end of the decade, entrusted to a deorbit vehicle that NASA has tasked SpaceX with building.

## The Shift

Point Nemo is often confused, in conversation, with another ocean record: that of the Mariana Trench, more than 11,000 meters below the surface at the bottom of Challenger Deep. Both are in the Pacific, both pass for extremes, but one measures a depth, the other a remoteness. The seafloor beneath Point Nemo is, in fact, nothing exceptional, barely 4,000 meters. It is not the vertical that makes the place special, it is the horizontal: its only quality is to turn its back on every coast, in all directions at once. A purely negative criterion, the absence of nearby land, is enough to make a point on the globe the most sought-after destination of the space industry.

repere.texte: Point Nemo is located at 48°52.6′S 123°23.6′W, about 2,688 km from the three nearest emerged lands: Ducie (Pitcairn), Motu Nui (Easter Island), and Maher Island (Antarctica).
repere.source: NOAA, National Ocean Service, “What is Point Nemo?”

carte.punch: About 2,688 km from the nearest land, Point Nemo serves as a graveyard for satellites.
carte.idee: Calculated in 1992, Point Nemo lies about 2,688 km from the three nearest lands. It is where debris is least likely to land on anyone: space agencies deorbit stations and satellites there, from Mir in 2001 to the ISS, planned by the end of the decade.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: Details Lukatela's calculation and its recalculation in 2022 with modern mapping data.

quiz.question: Why do space agencies aim for Point Nemo to deorbit end-of-life spacecraft?
choix: Because it is the deepest spot in the ocean, which swallows debris for good
Because it is the point in the ocean farthest from any inhabited land, which minimizes the risk to populations
Because an ocean current naturally gathers floating debris there, making it easier to recover
Because the seafloor there is too shallow to allow recovery, discouraging any looting
quiz.explication: Point Nemo is calculated as the point farthest from any emerged land (about 2,688 km), not as the deepest: that record belongs to the Mariana Trench. Keeping the reentry zone far from any inhabited land minimizes the risk that a piece of debris surviving atmospheric reentry will hit someone.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who calculated Point Nemo, and for what purpose, according to the entry?
choix: Hrvoje Lukatela, in 1992, to demonstrate the capabilities of spatial geometry software
NASA, in 2001, to prepare for the deorbiting of the Mir station
Alfred Russel Wallace, in 1856, during an expedition in the Pacific
The International Hydrographic Organization, in 2002, to redefine the limits of the oceans
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry attributes the calculation to the surveying engineer Hrvoje Lukatela, in 1992, who was seeking to demonstrate the capabilities of a software package on the longest swim problem.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What happened on March 23, 2001, according to the entry?
choix: The initial calculation of Point Nemo by Hrvoje Lukatela
The publication of NASA's transition report on the ISS
The deorbiting of the Russian station Mir near Point Nemo
The recalculation of Point Nemo with modern mapping data
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry dates to March 23, 2001 the deorbiting of the Mir station, most of whose 130 tons disintegrated, the rest being visible from Fiji.
